segments.source: Having traced the historical development of logic, we now turn our attention to its core concepts. In this section, we'll explore the building blocks of formal logic: propositions, logical operators, truth tables, and the principles of valid reasoning. These fundamental ideas form the foundation upon which all logical analysis is built. Let's begin with the concept of propositions. In logic, a proposition is a declarative statement that is either true or false. It's the basic unit of logical analysis, the atom from which more complex logical structures are built. Consider these examples:
segments.translation: După ce am urmărit dezvoltarea istorică a logicii, ne îndreptăm acum atenția către conceptele sale de bază. În această secțiune vom explora elementele constitutive ale logicii formale: propozițiile, operatorii logici, tabelele de adevăr și principiile raționamentului valid. Aceste idei fundamentale stau la baza oricărei analize logice. Să începem cu noțiunea de propoziție. În logică, o propoziție este un enunț declarativ care este fie adevărat, fie fals. Ea este unitatea de bază a analizei logice, atomul din care se construiesc structuri logice mai complexe. Să luăm aceste exemple:

segments.source: "Paris is the capital of France." "The moon is made of cheese." "All prime numbers are odd."
segments.translation: „Parisul este capitala Franței.” „Luna este făcută din brânză.” „Toate numerele prime sunt impare.”

segments.source: Each of these statements makes a claim that can be evaluated as either true or false. The first statement is true, the second is false, and the third is false (because 2 is an even prime number). It's important to note that not all sentences are propositions. Questions, commands, and exclamations are not propositions because they don't make claims that can be evaluated as true or false. For instance: "What time is it?" (This is a question, not a statement)
segments.translation: Fiecare dintre aceste enunțuri face o afirmație ce poate fi evaluată ca adevărată sau falsă. Primul este adevărat, al doilea fals, iar al treilea fals (pentru că 2 este un număr prim par). Este important de reținut că nu toate frazele sunt propoziții. Întrebările, poruncile și exclamațiile nu sunt propoziții, fiindcă nu formulează afirmații evaluabile ca adevărate sau false. De pildă: „Cât e ceasul?” (Aceasta este o întrebare, nu un enunț.)

segments.source: "Please close the door." (This is a command, not a statement) "Wow, what a beautiful day!" (This is an exclamation, not a statement) Similarly, sentences that contain variables or are context-dependent may not be propositions in themselves. For example: "X + 5 = 10" (This is an equation, not a proposition. Its truth value depends on the value of X) "He is tall." (Without context specifying who "he" is, we can't evaluate this as true or false) Understanding what constitutes a proposition is crucial because propositions are the basic elements that we manipulate in logical reasoning. Propositions can be simple (also called atomic) or compound (also called molecular). Simple propositions cannot be broken down further into other propositions. Compound propositions, on the other hand, are formed by combining simple propositions using logical connectives or operators. This brings us to our next fundamental concept: logical operators. The most common logical operators are: Negation (¬): This operator flips the truth value of a proposition. If p is a proposition, then ¬p is read as "not p." For example, if p is "It is raining," then ¬p is "It is not raining." Conjunction (∧): This operator combines two propositions with an "and." If p and q are propositions, then p ∧ q is read as "p and q." For example, if p is "It is cold" and q is "It is windy," then p ∧ q is "It is cold and windy." segments.source: q." In logic, this is an inclusive or, meaning it's true if either or both propositions are true. For example, if p is "I will study math" and q is "I will study logic," then p ∨ q means "I will study math or logic (or both)." Implication (→): This operator represents an "if...then" relationship between propositions. If p and q are propositions, then p → q is read as "if p, then q" or "p implies q." For example, if p is "It rains" and q is "The ground gets wet," then p → q means "If it rains, then the ground gets wet." Biconditional (↔): This operator represents an "if and only if" relationship between propositions. If p and q are propositions, then p ↔ q is read as "p if and only if q." For example, if p is "A triangle has three sides" and q is "A triangle has three angles," then p ↔ q means "A shape is a triangle if and only if it has three sides and three angles." These operators allow us to construct complex logical statements from simple ones. But how do we determine the truth value of these complex statements? This is where truth tables come in. Truth tables are a powerful tool for analyzing the behavior of logical operators and evaluating the truth values of compound propositions. A truth table shows all possible combinations of truth values for the component propositions and the resulting truth value of the compound proposition.
